{{Legend0|#D3D3D3|No election}} }} '''United States gubernatorial elections''' were held on November 5, 2019, in [[2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election|Kentucky]] and [[2019 Mississippi gubernatorial election|Mississippi]], and on October 12, 2019, with a runoff on November 16, in [[2019 Louisiana gubernatorial election|Louisiana]]. These elections formed part of the [[2019 United States elections]]. The last regular gubernatorial elections for all three states were in [[2015 United States gubernatorial elections|2015]]. The Democrats had to defend an incumbent in Louisiana, while the Republicans had to defend an incumbent in Kentucky plus an open seat in Mississippi. Though all three seats up were in typically [[red states and blue states|Republican states]], the election cycle became unexpectedly competitive: Kentucky and Louisiana were seen as highly contested races; and Mississippi's race ultimately became closer than usual, despite being seen as favorable for the Republicans. Democrats were able to hold their seat in Louisiana and flip the governor's seat in Kentucky, while Republicans successfully kept the Mississippi governorship by winning the open seat. As a result, the Democrats gained a net of one seat, bringing the total number of Democratic governors to 24, while Republicans were reduced to 26 governors, continuing a streak of governor's seat gains by Democrats made under Republican [[President of the United States|President]] [[Donald Trump]] that began in [[2017 United States gubernatorial elections|2017]]. This is the first time since [[2003 United States gubernatorial elections|2003]] in which a party made a net gain of seats in this cycle of governorships, and the first time since [[1991 United States gubernatorial elections|1991]] that Kentucky and Louisiana elected candidates of the same party. Democrats also won the total popular vote for gubernatorial elections for the third year in a row, and for the first time since 1991 in this cycle of governorships, albeit by an extremely narrow margin of 320 votes, or 0.01%. Additionally, these are the first gubernatorial elections since [[1981 United States gubernatorial elections|1981]] in which all of the margins of victory were under ten points. Until [[2026 United States gubernatorial elections|2026]], this was the last time an incumbent Republican governor lost re-election. It is also the last time where the Democrats won the governorship in Louisiana. ==Pre-election composition== [[Kentucky]] and [[Louisiana]] were seen as the two competitive races in this cycle. Kentucky governor [[Matt Bevin]] had very low approval ratings over issues such as Medicare expansion, pensions, and education. Bevin was the least popular governor in the United States, with only a 33% approval rating, in April 2019.{{Cite web|url=https://www.governing.com/archive/gov-kentucky-governor-primary-gubernatorial-trump-election-results.html|title=Why America's Least Popular Governor Will Likely Get Reelected|author=Alan Greenblatt|date=May 20, 2019|website=Governing}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/29/us/politics/matt-bevin-andy-beshear-kentucky-governor.html|title=Kentucky Governor's Race Tests Impact of Impeachment in States|first=Jonathan|last=Martin|date=October 29, 2019|work=The New York Times}}{{cite news |last=Craven |first=Julia |date=November 6, 2019 |title=Beshear Beats Bevin in Kentucky Governor's Race |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/kentucky-governors-race-andy-beshear-defeats-incumbent-matt-bevin.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106023110/https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/kentucky-governors-race-andy-beshear-defeats-incumbent-matt-bevin.html |archive-date=November 6, 2019 |access-date=November 6, 2019 |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |language=en}} When teachers walked out to protest education funding, Bevin blamed them for [[child molestation]] and called them "selfish thugs".{{cite news|title=Matt Bevin's defeat in Kentucky wasn't just about him|url=https://www.vox.com/2019/11/6/20951510/matt-bevin-kentucky-governor-loss-beshear-medicaid-teacher|last=Golshan|first=Tara|publisher=Vox|access-date=November 30, 2019}} Bevin also attempted to roll back the state's Medicare expansion, which would've lead to 500,000 people in the state losing their health insurance, and the measure was deeply unpopular in Kentucky and never passed.{{cite news|title= Democrats make Medicaid center of Kentucky governor fight|url=https://thehill.com/policy/healthcare/446756-dems-make-medicaid-center-of-kentucky-governor-fight|last=Weixel|first=Nathan|publisher=The Hill|access-date=November 30, 2019}} In Louisiana, Democratic incumbent [[John Bel Edwards]] was popular in the deep red state, as he had worked across the aisle with a number of issues such as abortion. Edwards also brought Medicaid expansion to the state, a move that garnered praise and was popular.{{cite news|title=In Blow To Trump's Medicaid Policies, Democrat Wins In Louisiana|url=https://www.forbes.com/sites/brucejapsen/2019/11/16/in-blow-to-trumps-medicaid-policies-democrat-wins-in-louisiana/#2a532ade1d4f|last=Jaspen|first=Bruce|work=Forbes|access-date=November 30, 2019}} Even though Edwards was popular, the sheer amount of Republicans in the state made the race competitive. [[Mississippi]], whose governor was term-limited, was one of the most Republican states in the country and hadn't voted a Democrat as governor since 1999, and Republican [[Tate Reeves]] was a long serving public servant in the state. However, a formidable campaign by Democrat [[Jim Hood]] made the race closer than initially expected. Hood made bringing Medicaid expansion to Mississippi the central issue of his campaign, which resonated with voters in the state as many people wanted improvements to health care.{{cite news|title=Mississippi Governor Election Preview|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/11/01/775305580/mississippi-governor-election-preview|last=Inskeep|first=Steve|publisher=NPR|access-date=November 30, 2019}} ==Election predictions== Several sites and individuals publish predictions of competitive seats. These predictions look at factors such as the strength of the [[incumbent]] (if the incumbent is running for re-election), the strength of the candidates, and the partisan leanings of the state (reflected in part by the state's [[Cook Partisan Voting Index]] rating). The predictions assign ratings to each state, with the rating indicating the predicted advantage that a party has in winning that seat. Most election predictors use: * "tossup": no advantage * "tilt" (used by some predictors): advantage that is not quite as strong as "lean" * "lean": slight advantage * "likely": significant, but surmountable, advantage * "safe" or "solid": near-certain chance of victory {|class="wikitable sortable" |+ !State ![[Cook Partisan Voting Index|PVI]] ! Bevin conceded on November 14,{{cite news|url=https://www.wlky.com/article/its-recanvass-day-in-kentucky-how-it-works-beshear-bevin-governor/29796544|title=Gov. Matt Bevin won't contest results, concedes from gubernatorial race|publisher=WLKY|date=14 November 2019|access-date=14 November 2019}} after a recanvass took place that day{{cite news|url=https://www.newsweek.com/gov-matt-bevin-refuses-concede-kentucky-race-even-after-secretary-state-calls-it-democrat-andy-1469998|title=Gov. Bevin Officially Requests Recanvass Of Election Results|last=Barton|first=Ryland|date=2019-11-06|website=NPR.org|language=en|access-date=2019-11-07}} that did not materially change the vote count. [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] John Hicks also qualified for the ballot and received 2% of the vote. Statewide turnout was just over 42%,{{cite news|title=Voter turnout tops 41 percent in tight race for Kentucky governor|url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article236988299.html|last=ACQUISTO|first=Alex|publisher=Lexington Herald Leader|access-date=November 5, 2019}} much higher than for the [[2015 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2015 gubernatorial election]]. The result was a major swing from 2016, when [[Donald Trump]] won the state by 30 points and Republicans gained a supermajority in both chambers of the [[Kentucky General Assembly]]. {{Election box Edwards became the first Louisiana Democrat to secure consecutive terms since [[Edwin Edwards]] (no relation to John Bel Edwards) in [[1975 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1975]]. It was the closest Louisiana gubernatorial election since 1979. Under Louisiana's [[Louisiana primary|jungle primary]] system, all candidates appear on the same ballot, regardless of party, and voters may vote for any candidate, regardless of their party affiliation. Because no candidate received an absolute majority of the vote during the primary election on October 12, 2019, a runoff election was held on November 16, 2019, between the top two candidates in the primary, Edwards and Rispone.{{cite web |url=https://www.sos.la.gov/ElectionsAndVoting/PublishedDocuments/ElectionsCalendar2019.pdf|title=Elections Calendar 2019|work= www.sos.la.gov |access-date=March 13, 2023}} Louisiana is the only state that has a jungle primary system ([[California]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]] have a similar [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|top-two primary]] system). According to the [[Louisiana Secretary of State]] more than 384,000{{Cite web|url=https://electionstatistics.sos.la.gov/Data/Early_Voting_Statistics/Statewide/2019_1012_StatewideStats.pdf|title=Louisiana Secretary of State Statistics}} early votes were cast, a significant increase from the 2015 gubernatorial election in which 234,000{{Cite web|url=https://electionstatistics.sos.la.gov/Data/Early_Voting_Statistics/Statewide/2015_1024_StatewideStats.pdf|title=Louisiana Secretary of State Statistics}} early votes were cast. {{Election box begin no change| title=Louisiana blanket primary{{cite web |title=Unofficial Results |url=https://voterportal.sos.la.gov/Graphical |website=Louisiana Secretary of State |access-date=October 12, 2019}}}} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change| |party = Democratic Party (United States) |candidate = [[John Bel Edwards]] (incumbent) |votes = 625,970 |percentage = 46.59 }} {{Election box winning candidate with party link no change| |party = Republican Party (United States) |candidate = [[Eddie Rispone]] |votes = 368,319 |percentage = 27.42 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Republican Party (United States) |candidate = [[Ralph Abraham (politician)|Ralph Abraham]] |votes = 317,149 |percentage = 23.61 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Democratic Party (United States) |candidate = Oscar Dantzler |votes = 10,993 |percentage = 0.82 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Republican Party (United States) |candidate = Patrick Landry |votes = 10,966 |percentage = 0.82 }} {{Election box candidate with party link no change| |party = Independent (United States) |candidate = Gary Landrieu |votes = 10,084 |percentage = 0.75 }} {{Election box total no change |votes = 1,343,481 |percentage = 100.00 }} {{Election box end}} {{Election box begin| title=Louisiana general election{{cite web |title=Louisiana Secretary of State - '''Hood:''' {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} | title = [[Governor of Mississippi|Governor]] | before_election = [[Phil Bryant]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Tate Reeves]] | after_party = Republican Party (United States) }} Incumbent governor [[Phil Bryant]] was ineligible to run for a third term due to [[term limit]]s. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] nominated incumbent attorney general [[Jim Hood]], the only Democrat holding statewide office in Mississippi; the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated incumbent lieutenant governor [[Tate Reeves]] after a runoff. Situated in the [[Deep South]], [[Mississippi]] is one of the most Republican states in the country. No Democrat has been elected to the governorship since [[Ronnie Musgrove]] in [[1999 Mississippi gubernatorial election|1999]]. However, the state's Democratic Attorney General, Jim Hood, who had held his office since 2004 and had yet to lose a statewide election, put the Republican's winning streak of four elections in a row to the test, as the race became unusually competitive. Reeves defeated Hood in the general election by a margin of 5.1%, making this the closest a Democrat had come to winning a Mississippi gubernatorial election since 1999, where Musgrove won with 49.6% of the vote.{{Cite news |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2019/11/5/20947980/mississippi-governor-results-tate-reeves-republican |title=Republican Tate Reeves wins a surprisingly close 2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election.title: 2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election
2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election.text:
{{Short description|none}} {{for|related races|2019 United States gubernatorial elections}} {{Use American English|date=January 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=September 2023}} {{Infobox election | election_name = 2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election | country = Kentucky | type = presidential | ongoing = no | previous_election = 2015 Kentucky gubernatorial election | previous_year = 2015 | next_election = 2023 Kentucky gubernatorial election | next_year = 2023 | election_date = November 5, 2019 | image1 = Andy Beshear in January 2020 (2) (cropped).jpg | nominee1 = '''[[Andy Beshear]]''' | party1 = Democratic Party (United States) | popular_vote1 = '''709,890''' | percentage1 = '''49.19%''' | running_mate1 = '''[[Jacqueline Coleman]]''' | image2 = File:Matt Bevin (cropped).jpg | image_size = 150x150px | nominee2 = [[Matt Bevin]] | party2 = Republican Party (United States) | popular_vote2 = 704,754 | percentage2 = 48.84% | running_mate2 = [[Ralph Alvarado]] | map_image = {{switcher |[[File:2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election results map by county.svg|301px]] |County results |[[File:2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election results map by congressional district.svg|301px]] |Congressional district results |[[File:2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election results map by state senate district.svg|301px]] |State senate district results |[[File:2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election results map by state house district.svg|301px]] |State house district results |[[File:2019 Kentucky Gubernatorial Election by Precinct.svg|305px]] |Precinct results }} | map_size = 301px | map_caption = '''Beshear:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584CDE|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933E5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0D0596|>90%}}

'''Tie:''' {{legend0|#D2B1D9|40–50%}} {{legend0|#ae8bb1|50%}} {{legend0|#808080|No data}} | title = [[Governor of Kentucky|Governor]] | before_election = [[Matt Bevin]] | before_party = Republican Party (United States) | after_election = [[Andy Beshear]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) | turnout = 44.2% ({{increase}} 13.7 [[percentage_point|pp]]) }} {{ElectionsKY}} The '''2019 Kentucky gubernatorial election''' took place on November 5, 2019, to elect the [[Governor of Kentucky|governor]] and [[Lieutenant Governor of Kentucky|lieutenant governor]] of [[Kentucky]].{{cite web|url=https://ballotpedia.org/Kentucky_gubernatorial_and_lieutenant_gubernatorial_election,_2019|title=Kentucky gubernatorial and lieutenant gubernatorial election, 2019|website=Ballotpedia|language=en|access-date=2019-06-22|df=mdy-all}} The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] nominee, [[Andy Beshear]], defeated [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] incumbent governor [[Matt Bevin]]. It was the closest gubernatorial election since [[1915 Kentucky gubernatorial election|1915]], and was the closest race of the [[2019 United States gubernatorial elections|2019 gubernatorial election cycle]]. This was the only statewide victory in 2019 for Democrats in Kentucky. Beshear won by 0.37 percentage points, receiving 49.20% of the vote to Bevin's 48.83%.{{cite news|last=Coaston|first=Jane|date=November 8, 2019|title=Matt Bevin's Libertarian opponent says the Kentucky election just proved his point|work=[[Vox (website)|Vox]]|url=https://www.vox.com/2019/11/8/20953887/matt-bevin-andy-beshear-john-hicks-libertarian-kentucky|url-status=live|access-date=November 10, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210317080509/https://www.vox.com/2019/11/8/20953887/matt-bevin-andy-beshear-john-hicks-libertarian-kentucky|archive-date=March 17, 2021}} Bevin won 97 counties, while Beshear won 23 counties.{{Cite web|url=https://www.wkyt.com/content/news/WKYT-Interactive--Voter-turnout-for-2019-general-election-564563511.html|date=November 6, 2019|title= Voter turnout for 2019 general election|website=WKYT}} Beshear also carried only two of the state's six congressional districts, but those districts were the state's two most urbanized, the Louisville-based [[Kentucky's 3rd congressional district|3rd]] and the Lexington-based [[Kentucky's 6th congressional district|6th]].J. Miles Coleman. [https://twitter.com/jmilescoleman/status/1192238192147259392 "... Beshear carried #KY03 (Louisville) by 37% & #KY06 (metro Lexington) by 14%. He only won two CDs, but his districts also had the highest turnout. Beshear also kept #KY04 (Cincy suburbs) close,"] Twitter. Beshear won with overwhelming support in the major population hubs of [[Louisville, Kentucky|Louisville]] and [[Lexington, Kentucky|Lexington]] and their suburbs, as well as major vote swings in the Republican-leaning [[Cincinnati, Ohio|Cincinnati]] suburbs. Beshear was also aided by Bevin's lackluster performance in counties that had previously been swinging heavily towards Republicans, particularly the coal country of Eastern Kentucky, where Beshear won multiple counties that overwhelmingly voted Republican in [[2016 United States presidential election in Kentucky|2016]].{{cite news|title=Democrat Andy Beshear just unseated Kentucky's Trump-loving governor Matt Bevin|url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2019/11/5/20949770/kentucky-governor-election-results-andy-beshear|last=Golshan|first=Tara|publisher=Vox|access-date=November 5, 2019}} Voter turnout was high across the state compared to past Kentucky elections, with a statewide turnout of about 42%. Fayette County (Lexington) saw a 20% increase in voter turnout, and Beshear received over twice as many votes in the county than the 2015 Democratic nominee for governor, [[Jack Conway (politician)|Jack Conway]]. Unusually high turnout was seen as a major factor in Beshear's win. Beshear's win coincided with Democratic momentum nationwide in elections in 2017, 2018, and 2019, following the [[2016 United States presidential election|election of Donald Trump in 2016]].{{cite news|last=Rocha|first=Veronica|date=November 6, 2019|title=Election day in Kentucky, Mississippi and Virginia|publisher=[[CNN]]|url=https://www.cnn.com/politics/live-news/2019-election-results-kentucky-mississippi-virginia/index.html|access-date=November 5, 2019}} However, Republicans won all other statewide races in Kentucky in 2019, including the attorney general and secretary of state offices which Democrats had held going into the election.{{cite news|last=Sonka|first=Joe|date=November 5, 2019|title=Daniel Cameron wins Kentucky attorney general race in historic victory|work=[[The Courier-Journal]]|url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2019/11/05/kentucky-election-results-2019-cameron-wins-attorney-general-race/4155926002/|url-status=live|url-access=limited|access-date=November 11, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20210612002751/https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2019/11/05/kentucky-election-results-2019-cameron-wins-attorney-general-race/4155926002/|archive-date=June 12, 2021}} Bevin conceded on November 14,{{cite news|date=November 14, 2019|title=Gov. Matt Bevin won't contest results, concedes from gubernatorial race|publisher=[[WLKY]]|url=https://www.wlky.com/article/its-recanvass-day-in-kentucky-how-it-works-beshear-bevin-governor/29796544|url-status=live|access-date=November 14, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210316074757/https://www.wlky.com/article/its-recanvass-day-in-kentucky-how-it-works-beshear-bevin-governor/29796544|archive-date=March 16, 2021}} after a recanvass took place that day{{cite news|url=https://www.newsweek.com/gov-matt-bevin-refuses-concede-kentucky-race-even-after-secretary-state-calls-it-democrat-andy-1469998|title=Gov. Matt Bevin refuses to concede Kentucky race, even after Secretary of State calls it for Democrat Andy Beshear|last=Lemieux|first=Melissa|date=November 5, 2019|work=Newsweek|access-date=6 November 2019}}{{Cite news|last=Barton|first=Ryland|date=November 6, 2019|title=Kentucky GOP Gov. Bevin Officially Requests Recanvass Of Election Results|website=[[Morning Edition]]|publisher=[[NPR]]|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/11/06/776937037/kentucky-gop-gov-bevin-officially-requests-recanvass-of-election-results|url-status=live|access-date=November 7, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210119204346/https://www.npr.org/2019/11/06/776937037/kentucky-gop-gov-bevin-officially-requests-recanvass-of-election-results|archive-date=January 19, 2021}} that did not change the vote count. [[Libertarian Party (United States)|Libertarian]] John Hicks also qualified for the ballot and received 2% of the vote. Statewide turnout was just over 42%,{{cite news|last1=Acquisto|first1=Alex|last2=Patton|first2=Janet|date=November 5, 2019|title=Voter turnout tops 41 percent in tight race for Kentucky governor|work=[[Lexington Herald-Leader]]|url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article236988299.html|url-status=live|url-access=limited|access-date=November 5, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210130182720/https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article236988299.html|archive-date=January 30, 2021}} much higher than for the [[2015 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2015 gubernatorial election]]. ==Background== Major-party primary elections occurred on May 21, 2019.{{Cite web|url=https://elect.ky.gov/calendar/Documents/2019%20Election%20Calendar.pdf|title=2019 Kentucky Election Calendar}} Incumbent [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] governor [[Matt Bevin]] was renominated by the Republican Party. Kentucky Attorney General [[Andy Beshear]] won the Democratic nomination with 37.9% of the vote in a three-way contest, in which due to his father he had the greatest name recognition.{{Cite news|last=Desrochers|first=Daniel|date=May 21, 2019|title=It's Beshear vs. Bevin. 11, 2021}} No Republican governor of Kentucky has ever been elected to more than one term, even after the state's constitutional prohibition of governors serving consecutive terms was repealed in 1992. The only Republican before Bevin to run for reelection, [[Ernie Fletcher]], was defeated by [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democrat]] [[Steve Beshear]] in [[2007 Kentucky gubernatorial election|2007]] (Steve Beshear is the father of Bevin's Democratic challenger, Andy). Bevin was the second Republican governor of Kentucky in the last 50 years. Andy Beshear was the first governor of Kentucky to be a direct relative of a former governor. Beshear had the support of 2020 Senate candidate [[Amy McGrath]], his father and former governor [[Steve Beshear]], former governor [[Paul E. Patton|Paul Patton]], and representative and primary challenger [[Rocky Adkins]], all well-known Democrats in the state. Bevin had the support of President [[Donald Trump]], who remained relatively popular in the state, particularly in rural areas. Trump and US senator [[Rand Paul]] held a rally in support of Bevin and Republican [[Attorney General of Kentucky|Attorney General]] nominee [[Daniel Cameron (Kentucky politician)|Daniel Cameron]] the day before the election. Many considered the decisive factor in this election whether voters would vote based on local issues, as Bevin and his policies were deeply unpopular,{{cite news|last=Aulbach|first=Lucas|date=July 18, 2019|title=With an election months away, Matt Bevin again ranked least popular governor in the US|work=[[The Courier-Journal]]|url=https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2019/07/18/kentucky-governor-matt-bevin-least-popular-again-morning-consult-poll/1764726001/|url-status=live|url-access=limited|access-date=November 5, 2019|archive-url=https://archive.today/20210612001635/https://www.courier-journal.com/story/news/politics/2019/07/18/kentucky-governor-matt-bevin-least-popular-again-morning-consult-poll/1764726001/|archive-date=June 12, 2021}} or as a referendum on Trump, with whom Bevin closely aligned. The former would be more favorable for Democrats, the latter for Republicans. Bevin was the least popular governor in the United States, with a 33% approval rating in April 2019.{{Cite web|url=https://www.governing.com/archive/gov-kentucky-governor-primary-gubernatorial-trump-election-results.html|title=Why America's Least Popular Governor Will Likely Get Reelected|author=Alan Greenblatt|date=May 20, 2019|website=Governing}}{{Cite web|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2019/10/29/us/politics/matt-bevin-andy-beshear-kentucky-governor.html|title=Kentucky Governor's Race Tests Impact of Impeachment in States|first=Jonathan|last=Martin|date=October 29, 2019|work=The New York Times}}{{cite news |last=Craven |first=Julia |date=November 6, 2019 |title=Beshear Beats Bevin in Kentucky Governor's Race |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/kentucky-governors-race-andy-beshear-defeats-incumbent-matt-bevin.html |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191106023110/https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/kentucky-governors-race-andy-beshear-defeats-incumbent-matt-bevin.html |archive-date=November 6, 2019 |access-date=November 6, 2019 |work=[[Slate (magazine)|Slate]] |language=en}} ==Republican primary== ===Candidates=== ====Nominated==== *[[Matt Bevin]], incumbent governor of Kentucky{{cite news|last1=Bailey|first1=Phillip M.|date=January 25, 2019|title='I chose to run with Sen. fifth Tuesday following the election (December 10).{{cite news|url=https://time.com/5719595/kentucky-governor-race-matt-bevin-recount/|title=Democrat Andy Beshear Has Declared Victory in Tight What happens next?|first=Daniel|last=Desrochers|publisher=Lexington Herald Leader|date=November 6, 2019|access-date=November 6, 2019}} While a recount law does exist in Kentucky, it does not permit recounts for gubernatorial elections.{{cite web|url=https://www.uky.edu/electionlaw/analysis/kentuckys-post-election-procedure-close-races-2019-ky-gov-edition|title=Kentucky's Post Election Procedure in Close Races (2019 KY Gov Edition)|publisher=University of Kentucky|access-date=November 6, 2019}} Should a candidate contest the election results, the state legislature would determine the winner after hearing a report from a randomly selected 11-member committee from the House (8) and Senate (3). This process, which is enforced through the [[William Goebel#Goebel Election Law|Goebel Election Law]], has only been used once, during the [[1899 Kentucky gubernatorial election]].{{cite news |url=https://slate.com/news-and-politics/2019/11/matt-bevin-andy-beshear-trump-stolen-kentucky-election.html |title=Could Matt Bevin Steal the Kentucky Governor's Election? |website=Slate recanvass did not go in his favor.{{cite news|url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/article237113614.html|title=Republicans urge Bevin to provide proof of election fraud or "let it go" and concede|first=Daniel|last=Desrochers|publisher=Lexington Herald Leader|date=November 7, 2019|access-date=November 13, 2019}} On November 11, U.S. Senate Majority Leader [[Mitch McConnell]], a Kentucky Republican, announced that "all indications are" Beshear would be the next governor.{{cite news|url=https://www.courier-journal.com/get-access/?return=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.courier-journal.com%2Fstory%2Fnews%2Fpolitics%2F2019%2F11%2F11%2Fmcconnell-says-indications-are-beshear-will-be-governor%2F2562844001%2F|title=Mitch McConnell:'All indications are' Andy Beshear will be Kentucky governor|publisher=Louisville Courier Journal|date=November 11, 2019|access-date=November 11, 2019}} The recanvass did not result in any changes in the vote totals for either Beshear or Bevin, but found an additional vote for write-in candidate Blackii Effing Whyte. Bevin carried 97 of Kentucky's 120 counties. However, Beshear swamped Bevin in urban areas. Beshear carried the state's two largest counties, [[Jefferson County, Kentucky|Jefferson]] and [[Fayette County, Kentucky|Fayette]]–home to Louisville and Lexington, respectively–with over 60 percent of the vote. He also narrowly carried two of the three counties that make up the traditionally conservative Cincinnati suburbs, [[Kenton County, Kentucky|Kenton]] and [[Campbell County, Kentucky|Campbell]].{{cite web|url=https://elect.ky.gov/results/2010-2019/Documents/2019%20General%20Certified%20Results.pdf|title=Official 2019 Election Results|website=ky.gov|access-date=15 March 2020}} === Recanvassing === Beshear declared victory after the initial vote count,{{cite news|last1=Sullivan|first1=Kate|last2=Bradner|first2=Eric|date=November 6, 2019|title=Democrat Andy Beshear Claims Victory in Kentucky Governor Race|publisher=[[CNN]]|url=https://www.cnn.com/2019/11/05/politics/election-night-kentucky-virginia/index.html|url-status=live|access-date=November 5, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210213023934/https://www.cnn.com/2019/11/05/politics/election-night-kentucky-virginia/index.html|archive-date=February 13, 2021}} selecting J. Michael Brown to lead his transition team.{{cite news|last=Beshearky|first=Andy|date=November 6, 2019|title=Beshear announces J. Michael Brown will lead his transition team|work=[[Lexington Herald-Leader]]|url=https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/election/article237069309.html|url-status=live|url-access=limited|access-date=November 6, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201116070145/https://www.kentucky.com/news/politics-government/election/article237069309.html|archive-date=November 16, 2020}} Bevin refused to concede and requested a recanvassing of the vote, which took place on November 14. A recanvassing is a reprint of the voting receipts from each voting machine and is done to make sure county officials recorded vote totals correctly. It is not a recount, which the Kentucky State Constitution does not permit for gubernatorial races. The recanvass resulted in only one change, an additional vote for Independent candidate Blackii Effing Whyte, and Bevin conceded that day. With the recanvass producing no change in his vote total, Bevin conceded the race on November 14. Beshear was sworn in as governor on December 10, 2019.{{cite news|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/470510-bevin-concedes-defeat-in-kentucky-governors-race|title=Bevin concedes in Kentucky governor's race|first=Reid|last=Wilson|work=The Hill|date=November 14, 2019|access-date=November 14, 2019}} ==See also== *[[2019 United States elections]] *[[2019 Kentucky elections]] ==Notes== {{notelist}} '''Partisan clients'''

51.0% {{increase}} (runoff) | title = Governor | before_election = [[John Bel Edwards]] | before_party = Democratic Party (United States) | after_election = [[John Bel Edwards]] | after_party = Democratic Party (United States) }} {{Elections in Louisiana}} The '''2019 Louisiana gubernatorial election''' was held to elect the [[List of governors of Louisiana|governor of Louisiana]]. Incumbent [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor [[John Bel Edwards]] won re-election to a second term, defeating [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] businessman [[Eddie Rispone]]. Edwards became the first Democratic governor of Louisiana to win re-election to a second consecutive term in 44 years since [[Edwin Edwards]] (no relation) in [[1975 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1975]]. It was the closest Louisiana gubernatorial election since [[1979 Louisiana gubernatorial election|1979]]. This was the only Democratic-held governorship up for election in 2019 that [[Donald Trump]] won in the [[2016 United States presidential election|2016 presidential election]], and was the only statewide victory in 2019 for Democrats in Louisiana. Under Louisiana's [[Louisiana primary|jungle primary]] system, all candidates appear on the same ballot, regardless of party, and voters may vote for any candidate regardless of their party affiliation. Because no candidate received an absolute majority of the vote during the primary election on October 12, 2019, a runoff election was held on November 16, 2019, between the top two candidates in the primary, Edwards and Rispone.{{cite web |url=https://www.sos.la.gov/ElectionsAndVoting/PublishedDocuments/ElectionsCalendar2019.pdf |title=2019 ELECTIONS |publisher=Louisiana Secretary of State}} Louisiana is the only state that has a jungle primary system ([[California]] and [[Washington (state)|Washington]] have a similar [[Nonpartisan blanket primary|top two primary]] system). == Background == On Edwards’ Inauguration Day in 2016, [[Louisiana House of Representatives|State House]] Republicans, in a break with tradition, elected their own speaker, Representative [[Taylor Barras]] of New Iberia, over Edwards' choice, Representative [[Walt Leger III|Walt Leger]] of New Orleans. This move was said to be orchestrated by House Republican chairman [[Lance Harris]], who was considered a potential gubernatorial 2019 candidate and was a frequent Edwards critic.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/legislature/article_1e1b57db-13d3-5822-b86f-62ed800f1ce3.html|title=In rarely seen twist, last-minute candidate Taylor Barras selected Louisiana House speaker|last=Ballard|first=Mark|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} Edwards and Republican Legislative leaders repeatedly clashed over budget, tax and spending measures. [[List of attorneys general of Louisiana|Attorney General]] [[Jeff Landry]], who won Louisiana’s governorship in 2023 when Edwards was term-limited, was perhaps Edwards' most prominent detractor, filing multiple lawsuits against the governor and frequently criticizing him in the media. The two disagreed the most on social policies, such as Landry's staunch opposition to Edwards' executive order providing protections for [[LGBT]] workers of state government and contractors.{{Cite news|url=http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2016/11/landry_edwards_court.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171213082309/http://www.nola.com/politics/index.ssf/2016/11/landry_edwards_court.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=December 13, 2017|title=John Bel Edwards, Jeff Landry head to court over LGBT issues: 4 things to know|work=NOLA.com|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en-US}} Landry also assumed the leadership of [[David Vitter]]'s Political Action Committee, the Louisiana Committee for a Republican Majority,{{Cite news|url=http://www.washingtontimes.com/news/2016/jul/10/analysis-jeff-landry-to-take-leadership-role-of-vi/|title=Analysis: Jeff Landry to take leadership role of Vitter PAC|newspaper=[[The Washington Times]]|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en-US}} the organisation that was widely considered instrumental to [[Clay Higgins]]' upset Congressional victory over [[Scott Angelle]] in 2016.{{Cite news|url=http://www.nola.com/elections/index.ssf/2016/12/clay_higgins_scott_angelle.html|title=Louisiana congressional race: Career public servant vs. YouTube star|work=NOLA.com|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en-US}} Landry has closely aligned with [[President of the United States|President]] [[Donald Trump]] and attended Trump's 2017 [[State of the Union]] speech.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_6cf15a46-fdca-11e6-89b0-ab3108d71fca.html|title=AG Jeff Landry in Washington, D.C., with attorneys general group that met with President Donald Trump|last=Crisp|first=Elizabeth|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} Edwards also become a favorite target of U.S. representative [[Garret Graves]], a [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican]] from Baton Rouge and former aide to Governor [[Bobby Jindal]]. Graves frequently criticized the governor during the state's response to the 2016 August floods in the state. The two notably sparred during a hearing of the [[United States House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform|House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform]], of which Graves is a member. Edwards' aides called the exchange a "political ambush" while Graves accused the governor of lying.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_e3687fb2-25f5-11e7-a76d-e78fe64733a4.html|title=U.S. Rep. Garret Graves, Gov. John Bel Edwards sniping about flood recovery, again|last=Allen|first=Rebekah|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} Graves was also closely aligned with the [[First presidency of Donald Trump|Trump Administration]] and donated $300 to the [[first inauguration of Donald Trump|2017 Trump Inaugural]] fund.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_98cfe8e2-2581-11e7-ae4e-17f4b3ea8f74.html|title=Louisiana residents give more than $1M to Trump's inauguration|last=Crisp|first=Elizabeth|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} Graves also accompanied [[Vice President of the United States|Vice President]] [[Mike Pence]] during a visit to parts of the Baton Rouge area in May 2017.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_1942c3c8-40c6-11e7-9a50-737e283740df.html|title=VP Mike Pence vows 'Obamacare' repeal, touts budget plan and returns to flooded home during Louisiana trip|last=Crisp|first=Elizabeth|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} As the only [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic]] governor in the Deep South, Edwards and his agenda also been the target of numerous attacks from numerous groups affiliated with the national [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] such as America Rising and [[Americans for Prosperity]].{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_ca457f60-05d6-11e7-a4d5-2b2c4726b471.html|title=National GOP-backing group launches site against John Bel Edwards, 'The Accidental Governor'|last=Crisp|first=Elizabeth|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} Edwards, declared himself to be unbothered by these groups, and went on to classify them as "a Washington, D.C., political action committee, trying to bring the never-ending campaign cycle to Louisiana." Aware of their gubernatorial ambitions, Edwards and his aides repeatedly spoofed both U.S. senator [[John Kennedy (Louisiana politician)|John Neely Kennedy]] and Landry during their traditional response skits at Baton Rouge's Gridiron Show.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_a0b9df57-8899-5b2a-a3e9-4601981d36a3.html|title=Who stayed? Who went? Who never left? People, groups, things after Gov. John Bel Edwards took over|last=Bridges|first=Tyler|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} According to fundraising reports filed in 2016, Edwards had raised close to $3.3 million for his 2019 re-election effort.{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/elections/article_b7e7eb34-df5f-11e6-9449-037ae02d2837.html|title=Gov. John Bel Edwards, once long-shot candidate, building war chest ahead of 2019 re-election campaign|last=Bridges|first=Tyler|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}}{{Cite news|url=http://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/news/politics/article_3cde5a8e-f46a-11e6-83a3-1bf842a96fd8.html|title=In 2019 governor's race, John Bel Edwards has hefty fundraising lead on potential challenger Jeff Landry|agency=Associated Press|work=The Advocate|access-date=May 30, 2017|language=en}} By comparison, Landry had $544,000 on hand for a potential future campaign. Graves and Kennedy had yet to form separate entities for statewide campaigns per Louisiana Law. In the summer of 2017, Lieutenant Governor [[Billy Nungesser]] announced that he would not be a candidate for governor in 2019, and had decided to run for re-election. Nungesser said that he had disclosed his plans to run for re-election to then Governor-elect John Bel Edwards during his transition period. '''Hood:''' {{legend0|#a5b0ff|40–50%}} {{legend0|#7996e2|50–60%}} {{legend0|#6674de|60–70%}} {{legend0|#584cde|70–80%}} {{legend0|#3933e5|80–90%}} {{legend0|#0d056c|>90%}} |Precinct results }} | flag_year = 2001 }} {{ElectionsMS}} The '''2019 Mississippi gubernatorial election''' took place on November 5, 2019, to choose the next [[List of governors of Mississippi|governor of Mississippi]].{{cite web|url=https://www.sos.ms.gov/Elections-Voting/Documents/VoterInformationGuide.pdf|title=Mississippi Voter Information Guide|website=State of Mississippi – Secretary of State|access-date=2018-09-06|archive-date=2018-09-06|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180906233716/https://www.sos.ms.gov/Elections-Voting/Documents/VoterInformationGuide.pdf|url-status=dead}} Incumbent Governor [[Phil Bryant]] was ineligible to run for a third term due to [[term limit]]s. The [[Democratic Party (United States)|Democratic Party]] nominated incumbent Attorney General [[Jim Hood]], the only Democrat holding statewide office in Mississippi; the [[Republican Party (United States)|Republican Party]] nominated incumbent Lieutenant Governor [[Tate Reeves]]. In the general election, Reeves defeated Hood by a margin of 5.08%, with Reeves significantly underperforming [[Donald Trump]], who won the state by 18 points in [[2016 United States presidential election in Mississippi|2016]]. This was the last gubernatorial election to be held under the state's [[electoral college]] system, which was abolished by a [[2020 Mississippi elections#Elimination of state electoral college|2020 referendum]]. ==Background== Situated in the [[Deep South]] as a [[Social conservatism|socially conservative]] [[Bible Belt]] state, [[Mississippi]] is one of the most Republican states in the country. No Democrat has been elected to the governorship since [[Ronnie Musgrove]] in [[1999 Mississippi gubernatorial election|1999]]. However, the state's Democratic Attorney General, Jim Hood, who had held his office since 2004 and had yet to lose a statewide election, put the Republicans' winning streak of four elections in a row to the test, as the race became unusually competitive. Reeves defeated Hood in the general election by a margin of 5.1%, making this the closest a Democrat had come to winning a Mississippi gubernatorial election since 1999. Hood pulled off the best performance by a Democrat since the [[2003 Mississippi gubernatorial election]], when fellow Democrat [[Ronnie Musgrove]] took 45.81% of the vote.{{Cite news |url=https://www.vox.com/policy-and-politics/2019/11/5/20947980/mississippi-governor-results-tate-reeves-republican |title=Republican Tate Reeves wins a surprisingly close race, becoming Mississippi's next governor |last=Collins |first=Sean |date=2019-11-05 |work=Vox |access-date=2019-11-06 |language=en}} Hood flipped the counties of [[Chickasaw County, Mississippi|Chickasaw]], [[Lafayette County, Mississippi|Lafayette]], [[Madison County, Mississippi|Madison]], [[Panola County, Mississippi|Panola]], and [[Warren County, Mississippi|Warren]], which had all voted for Republican [[Donald Trump]] in the [[2016 United States presidential election in Mississippi|2016 United States presidential election]]. Uniquely among the states, the [[Constitution of Mississippi]] at the time established a sort of [[electoral college]] at the state level. For the election of governor. Article 5, Section 140 of the state constitution stated that each state House district was to be assigned an electoral vote, and that a candidate running for governor must receive a majority of electoral votes (essentially, they must win a majority of state House districts) in addition to winning a majority of the popular vote in order to be elected governor.MS Const. art. V, § 140 Article 5, Section 141 of the state constitution stated that if no candidate won both a popular and electoral vote majority, the state [[Mississippi House of Representatives|House of Representatives]] would decide the winner, choosing from the two highest popular vote winners.MS Const. art. V, § 141. This provision came into play only one time in the state's history; Democratic candidate [[Ronnie Musgrove]] in the [[1999 Mississippi gubernatorial election|1999 gubernatorial election]] garnered a plurality, but not a majority; the House selected Musgrove.{{Cite news|url=https://thehill.com/homenews/state-watch/447505-legal-fight-over-jim-crow-era-law-upends-mississippi-governor-race/|title=Legal fight over Jim Crow-era law upends Mississippi governor race|last=Wilson|first=Reid|date=9 June 2019|work=The Hill|access-date=2 October 2019}} In the lead-up to the election, controversy emerged over these constitutional provisions establishing a state system of electoral votes, with a federal lawsuit claiming the provisions were racially biased.{{Cite news|url=https://www.npr.org/2019/09/24/763510668/black-voters-sue-over-mississippis-jim-crow-era-election-law|title=Black Voters Sue Over Mississippi's Jim Crow-Era Election Law|date=24 September 2019|work=NPR|access-date=2 October 2019}} These provisions were put in place with the 1890 Mississippi Constitution, itself established by the segregationist [[Redeemers]] and overturning the [[Reconstruction era|Reconstruction-era]] 1868 Constitution, as part of [[Jim Crow laws|Jim Crow Era]] policy to minimize the power of African Americans in politics. Because of this, as well as [[gerrymandering]] that packed African Americans into a small number of districts, the plaintiffs claied the provisions should be struck down on the basis of racial bias.
